name: Metadata and Ontologies
title: Metadata and Ontologies
answer: Metadata and ontologies in research data and repositories concern structured descriptions that make datasets, papers, models and tools findable, comparable and reusable. The scope includes schema design, controlled vocabularies, semantic typing, provenance records and cross-repository mapping. It covers both lightweight metadata such as title, author and date, and formal ontologies that define classes and relations in a domain. The work sits between library science, knowledge representation and data curation.

crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

sections.body: Metadata and ontologies in research data and repositories concern structured descriptions that make datasets, papers, models and tools findable, comparable and reusable. The scope includes schema design, controlled vocabularies, semantic typing, provenance records and cross-repository mapping. It covers both lightweight metadata such as title, author and date, and formal ontologies that define classes and relations in a domain. The work sits between library science, knowledge representation and data curation.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: This work runs on repository platforms, metadata registries, triple stores and graph databases, often alongside standard serialisations such as JSON-LD, RDF and OWL. Many repositories expose metadata through OAI-PMH or REST APIs, and some use SPARQL endpoints for ontology queries. The infrastructure is usually modest compared with model training, but it must handle versioning, persistent identifiers and frequent schema updates.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: Curators and domain experts define terms, align them with existing ontologies, and annotate records by hand or with assisted tooling. Automated extraction can pull metadata from papers and datasets, but human review remains common for correctness and disambiguation. Validation against schemas and reasoners checks consistency, while mapping tables connect local fields to shared vocabularies.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Metadata itself is often openly licensed, but it can reveal sensitive details about data subjects, research locations or unpublished work. Provenance records must show who created or changed a term, when, and under what authority, because bad mappings propagate across repositories. Governance includes versioning of ontologies, community review of vocabulary changes, and clear policies on reuse and attribution.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: Metadata and ontologies are moving toward more machine actionable, linked and decentralised forms, with greater use of knowledge graphs and persistent identifiers. Large language models are being tested for metadata extraction and ontology alignment, but their output still needs human validation against source records. The likely direction is tighter coupling between repositories, automated crosswalks, and richer provenance that supports reproducibility and audit.
